analysis.one_liner: Protects and pays workers who report lawbreaking by companies the FTC regulates.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on November 13, 2024, sent to two House committees, and never received a hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give legal protection and cash awards to people who report violations of laws the Federal Trade Commission enforces. Workers could sue employers who fire, demote, or harass them for blowing the whistle, could not be forced into arbitration for those claims, and could collect 10 to 30 percent of any penalty over $1 million that their tip helps the FTC collect. The bill never moved after it was introduced; it died quietly in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, contractors, and subcontractors at companies under FTC jurisdiction who report violations would gain protection from retaliation, the right to a jury trial, triple back pay if they win, and awards of 10-30% of monetary sanctions when their information leads to enforcement collecting over $1 million. Consumers also benefit indirectly, since more internal wrongdoing would reach the FTC.

how_it_helps.text: Bars covered companies from firing, demoting, suspending, threatening, or harassing anyone who reports a suspected FTC-enforced violation, participates in an FTC investigation, or refuses to take part in suspected illegal activity [S2].

Lets whistleblowers sue in federal court with a jury trial, recover reinstatement, triple back pay with interest, and attorneys' fees, and explicitly voids predispute arbitration clauses and noncompete-type restrictions for these claims [S2].

Requires the FTC to pay an award of 10 to 30 percent of monetary sanctions (when a covered action collects over $1 million) to insiders whose original information leads to successful enforcement, paid from a fund built out of collected penalties rather than taxpayer appropriations [S2].

Blocks companies from using confidentiality or non-disparagement agreements to stop workers from communicating with the FTC, law enforcement, or Congress, and requires the FTC to keep whistleblower identities confidential [S2].
Extends protection to contractors and subcontractors at any tier, not just direct employees, and provides immunity from civil and criminal liability for protected disclosures [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Companies subject to FTC jurisdiction would bear the cost: new exposure to retaliation lawsuits, triple-damages awards, voided arbitration and confidentiality agreements, and larger chances that internal misdeeds trigger federal penalties. No taxpayer appropriation is required because awards are paid from collected sanctions.

drawbacks.text: A mandatory award program of 10-30% of large penalties could encourage speculative or opportunistic tips, and companies would face internal reports escalating directly to federal enforcement even for good-faith disputes [S2].

The bill overrides predispute arbitration agreements and certain restrictive covenants for these claims, which employers and business groups generally argue increases litigation costs and takes away a forum they see as faster and cheaper [S2].
The covered scope is very broad — any violation of any law, rule, or regulation the FTC enforces — which expands the FTC's whistleblower apparatus well beyond its most consumer-facing cases [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to workers and consumers are real and the direct fiscal cost to the public is small, since awards are paid out of collected penalties. The honest tradeoff is on the business side: broad coverage and mandatory awards would increase litigation and enforcement pressure on regulated companies, and some of that cost is passed to consumers through prices. On balance the design follows the model of the SEC and CFTC whistleblower programs, which have produced substantial enforcement recoveries.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Education and Workforce and Energy and Commerce committees, and neither committee ever held a hearing or vote on it before the 118th Congress ended, so it died without any floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the FTC Whistleblower Act of 2024 on November 13, 2024, joined by Rep. Lori Trahan as its only cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies subject to FTC jurisdiction are better off: they avoided a new regime of retaliation lawsuits, voided arbitration and confidentiality agreements, and mandatory awards for insiders whose tips trigger penalties.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and no Republican supported the bill; no vote ever occurred, so no partisan voting pattern exists.

industries.industry: Companies subject to FTC jurisdiction (advertising, consumer finance, tech platforms, retail)
industries.note: The bill would expose these companies to retaliation suits with triple back pay, void arbitration and confidentiality shields for whistleblower claims, and pay insiders 10-30% of penalties for tips that trigger enforcement. Their interest in blocking it runs against workers who report wrongdoing and the consumers those workers protect.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and employer-side defense counsel
industries.note: The bill voids predispute arbitration agreements for whistleblower retaliation claims and guarantees jury trials, reducing the volume of these disputes routed to arbitration. It also expands litigation over FTC-enforced law.
